prompt: The payment provider has announced it will retire its current API in June. Is that a risk?

choices.text: No: an issue, so schedule it
choices.why: Right. It is certain and dated, so it goes into the backlog as work.
Nothing positive about it for the team.
Ownership does not change whether it is uncertain.
A certain event is not a risk; it is handled now.

prompt: Which of these is a well-formed risk statement, by the lesson?

choices.text: The database might be slow on Monday mornings
choices.why: It says nothing about what would be affected.
No cause, no event, no effect.

choices.text: One billing expert; their exit delays payment a month
choices.why: Right. Cause, event and effect, and each part points to a different response.

choices.text: Staff turnover across the whole company, every single year
choices.why: A noun phrase points at no response.

prompt: An open-source calendar library might already handle recurring appointments, saving days. What is that, by the PMBOK definition?

choices.why: Right. An uncertain event with a positive effect deserves the same attention as a threat.

choices.text: An assumption that must be documented in the charter
choices.why: It may start as an assumption; as an uncertain gain it is an opportunity.

choices.text: Not a risk, since nothing bad can happen
choices.why: Risks include positive effects.

choices.text: An issue, since it is about a library
choices.why: It is uncertain, so it is not an issue.

prompt: Why does a pre-mortem work better than asking 'what might go wrong?'

choices.why: Its output goes into the register.
Right. Explaining an imagined failure is easier than predicting one aloud, so people say what already worried them.
Length is not the reason.
Everybody takes part, privately first.

prompt: What does a RAID log keep together?

choices.why: Not what the letters stand for.
Not the RAID log.
Not the RAID log.
Right. Each kind tends to turn into another.

prompt: 'The provider's sandbox will be available from week one' appears in an estimate. Why does the lesson list it as a source of risk?

choices.why: Right. Listing assumptions makes them visible as risks.
It has not happened.
Not always; that is why it is uncertain.

choices.text: Estimates should never mention third parties
choices.why: They should, and say what they assume.

prompt: Match each register field to its purpose.

pairs.right: A person who watches the risk
The sign the risk is starting to happen

prompt: A risk is owned by 'the team'. What does the lesson say?

choices.why: Right. The owner must be a person, or nobody watches it.

choices.text: That is the best owner, since everybody watches it
choices.why: In practice nobody does.

choices.text: It should be owned by the sponsor instead
choices.why: The owner should be close to the risk.
The rule applies to every risk.

prompt: A team's register has two hundred entries and is reviewed once a year. What is the lesson's diagnosis?

choices.why: Right. Keep the few that matter prominent, and review at a regular event.
Length is not thoroughness; nobody can hold it in mind.
More structure does not fix staleness.

choices.text: It should be replaced by a matrix
choices.why: A matrix ranks; the register still needs reviewing.

prompt: Risk A has a 30% probability and a 10-day impact. What is its expected value in days?
What is the sum of the expected values of the four threats, in days?
Risk B has the largest impact of all, yet sits in the middle band of the matrix. Why?

choices.why: The figures are as given.

choices.text: Its low probability pulls the product down
choices.why: Right. A matrix can hide a rare catastrophe among nuisances.

choices.text: People risks do not go on the matrix
choices.why: Any risk can go on it.

choices.text: The matrix adds probability and impact
choices.why: It multiplies ranks.

prompt: What is the chance, in percent, that none of the four threats happens? Round to the nearest whole number.
Why is the 2-day expected value the wrong number to plan around for risk B?

choices.text: The probability is too low to matter
choices.why: Low probability with a large impact still matters.
The probability is not in question.

choices.text: If it happens it costs 20 days; nobody loses 2
choices.why: Right. Expected value sizes a reserve across many risks; a single large risk needs its own response.

choices.text: Expected values cannot be computed for people risks
choices.why: They can; it is just the wrong planning number here.

prompt: Match each threat response to an example.

pairs.right: Use a different, stable payment provider
A fixed-price contract with a supplier
Pair a second developer on billing
One day in the plan for a resubmission

right_distractors: Delete the risk from the register

prompt: Why does the team accept risk D, the app store rejection, instead of mitigating it?

choices.why: That would be transfer or escalation.

choices.text: Accepting is the default for every risk
choices.why: Each risk gets the response that fits it.
It is 20%.
Right. It keeps one day in the plan for a resubmission.

prompt: The team wraps the payment provider behind its own interface. What does the lesson ask it to check next?

choices.why: Unrelated.
Right. The wrapper is new code, with defects of its own.

choices.text: Whether to transfer it as well
choices.why: Possible, but not what the lesson asks next.
Mitigation reduces it; the response has risks of its own.

prompt: For opportunities, making sure the opportunity happens is called ___ it.
Why hold the contingency reserve centrally rather than spread across tasks?

choices.text: Tasks are not allowed to have estimates
choices.why: They have estimates; the reserve is separate.

choices.text: Only the sponsor may spend any reserve
choices.why: That is the management reserve.

choices.text: Spread out, it gets spent anyway
choices.why: Right. Held centrally, it is spent only when a risk materialises.

choices.text: It makes the estimate look smaller
choices.why: Appearance is not the reason.

prompt: Match each reserve to what it covers and who controls it.

pairs.right: Identified risks; held by the project
What nobody foresaw; held above the project

prompt: A risk sits on activity B of lesson 6's network, which has a day of slack. Does it need a share of the time reserve?

choices.text: More, since B is the slots API
choices.why: Its importance does not change the arithmetic of slack.
A delay longer than the slack makes it critical.

choices.text: Less: slack absorbs up to a day
choices.why: Right. Risks on the critical path deserve the reserve.

choices.text: Exactly as much as a critical activity
choices.why: Slack makes the difference.

prompt: What does Fairbanks's rule say about how much architecture a system deserves?

choices.text: None until the system is in production
choices.why: Then the risks have already struck.
That ignores the risk-driven part.

choices.text: As much as the risks require, and no more
choices.why: Right. Name the risks, and choose design work that reduces each.

choices.text: The same amount for every system
choices.why: The point is that it varies with risk.

prompt: Which responses does the lesson list for reducing technical risk? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: A guess, not a response to a named risk.
Yes.

choices.text: A load test against a realistic scenario
choices.why: Yes.
Yes.

prompt: How should 'the ORM may generate N+1 queries' be written for the sponsor's register?
hint: Cause, event, effect, in business terms.

choices.text: It should stay off the register as too technical
choices.why: Technical risks belong in the same register.
A noun points at no response.

choices.text: Exactly as the developers phrased it
choices.why: A sponsor cannot weigh it in that form.

choices.text: Slow booking, broken SLA, fix cost
choices.why: Right. That is a decision a sponsor can make.

prompt: Order the steps the lesson follows for a risk.
trap: The reserve is sized from the quantified risks, after responses are chosen.
